chunks: As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from Ṣafwān, from Manṣūr, from Abū ʿUbayda al-Ḥadhdhāʾ, from Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him), who said:

Nosebleed, vomiting, and probing [between the teeth] that causes blood to flow — when you are averse to something [and act under compulsion], it nullifies the wudu; but if you are not averse to it, it does not nullify the wudu.
This report is interpreted as indicating recommendation (istihbab), because we have already clarified that wudu is not required for it under any circumstance. And what follows also indicates this.

key_terms.التَّخْلِيلُ: probing/toothpicking between the teeth that draws blood (takhlil)
key_terms.الِاسْتِحْبَابِ: recommendation/desirability (istihbab) — a non-obligatory jurisprudential degree in Shia fiqh

ai.seo_question: Does nosebleed, vomiting, or toothpicking that draws blood nullify wudu according to Imam al-Sadiq in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith, transmitted through a chain reaching Imam Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq (AS) via Abū ʿUbayda al-Ḥadhdhāʾ, states that nosebleed, vomiting, and toothpicking that draws blood nullify the wudu when one acts under aversion or compulsion, but not otherwise. Shaykh al-Ṭūsī reconciles this with other reports that categorically deny wudu-invalidation from such events by reinterpreting it as indicating recommendation (istihbāb) rather than legal obligation.
